name: divination

attributes.attribute: a Roman writer who claimed Celts read entrails
a Roman writer who agreed with Tacitus
a rite where a poet dreamed the new king inside a bull's hide
a letter system used in divination

sources: MacCulloch, J. A. The Religion of the Ancient Celts. London: Constable, 1911, 247ff.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Seeing the future, divination, was a duty of the druids among the insular and continental Celts. Roman writers Tacitus and Strabo claimed Celts read the entrails of sacrificed humans. Both Romans had reason to paint their enemies as barbarians, so that evidence of human sacrifice is arguable. Less disputed are rites that used animals and the flight of birds. Irish sources show druids and bards read omens. Rituals used chanted words, called díchetal do chennaib, and object reading, called teinm laeda. They also used trance, called imbas forosnai, and the letters of ogham. A grand rite chose the king, when a poet ate uncooked meat and slept wrapped in a bull's hide to dream the ruler, a practice called bull-sleep. On pivot days such as Samhain, common people read the future in omens and dreams.

okr.objective: Describe the methods and contested evidence of Celtic divination.
key_results: Roman writers Tacitus and Strabo claimed Celts read the entrails of sacrifices.
Druids and bards used ritual chants, trance, and ogham letters for divination.
On pivot days such as Samhain, common people read the future in omens and dreams.
